text:
In late August 1854, a terrible illness struck the crowded streets of Soho, in London. Within days, hundreds of people living near Broad Street were dead. The disease was cholera, which causes violent vomiting and diarrhea, and which can kill a healthy adult in a single day by draining the body of its fluids. Nobody then understood where it came from.

The dominant belief among doctors and officials was the miasma theory. This held that diseases like cholera spread through bad air, the foul smells rising from rotting waste, sewers and swamps. The idea was not foolish. Londoners lived with appalling stench, and sickness did seem to cluster in the dirtiest districts. But it was wrong, and acting on it cost lives.

John Snow, a physician who lived a short walk from Broad Street, doubted it. Snow was a quiet, teetotal man who had made his name pioneering the use of anesthesia, and had personally given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth. He had also studied cholera in earlier outbreaks and reached an unfashionable conclusion. Cholera, he argued, was not breathed in. It was swallowed. Whatever caused it must be taken in with food or drink, and it attacked the intestines first, which seemed to him more consistent with something ingested than something inhaled. Few colleagues agreed. Germs were not yet an accepted idea, and nobody had seen the cholera bacterium in any convincing way.

When the outbreak erupted near his home, Snow saw a chance to test his theory. Rather than rely on opinion, he went door to door. He obtained the list of the dead from the registrar's office and began visiting the homes of the victims, asking where they had gotten their water. Many of the poor in Soho had no running water at home. They carried it from public pumps in the street, and Snow noticed that the deaths clustered around one pump in particular, on Broad Street.

He then drew a map. On a street plan of the neighborhood, he marked each death with a small black bar stacked at the address where it occurred. The bars piled up thickly around the Broad Street pump, and thinned out with distance. It was a striking picture, though Snow was careful to note that a map alone proved little, since people living close to the pump might be sick for many reasons. What persuaded him was the exceptions, the cases that did not fit the pattern.

A workhouse near the pump housed some five hundred inmates, yet very few of them died. Snow discovered that the workhouse had its own well and did not use the Broad Street pump. A brewery on the same street also escaped almost untouched. Its workers, it turned out, were given free beer and drank little water, and the brewery too had its own supply. Meanwhile, a woman who lived far from Soho, in Hampstead, died of cholera after her sons brought her bottles of water from the Broad Street pump, which she had grown to prefer for its taste. Another victim, a young girl nearby, had also been drinking from it. These stray cases, which the bad air theory could not explain, fit Snow's idea perfectly.

By the evening of September 7, Snow was convinced. He took his evidence to the local Board of Guardians, the officials who ran the parish. Skeptical, but unable to ignore the pattern he laid out, they agreed to act. The next day, the handle of the Broad Street pump was removed, so that no one could draw water from it. The outbreak was already fading by then, as many residents had fled the area and the deadliest days had passed, so the removal's exact effect has been debated ever since. But the symbolism endured, and the pump handle became the most famous image in the history of public health.

Snow was not finished. With the help of a local clergyman, Henry Whitehead, who initially doubted him but knew the neighborhood intimately, he kept searching for the original source of the contamination. Whitehead found that a baby living at 40 Broad Street had fallen ill with diarrhea just before the outbreak began, and that its family's waste had been emptied into a cesspool directly beside the pump's well. The brick lining of the well was cracked, and it was likely that the infant's illness had seeped into the drinking water. Whitehead became so convinced that he spent years afterward promoting Snow's view.

Remarkably, the authorities largely rejected Snow's conclusions at first. An official inquiry decided that the water was not to blame, and the pump was reopened. Snow died in 1858, aged only forty-five, still without general acceptance of his theory. Only later, as scientists identified the cholera bacterium and confirmed that germs cause disease, did his work receive its due.

Today Snow is remembered as a founder of modern epidemiology, the study of how disease spreads through populations. His method was simple and powerful. He gathered the facts, mapped them, hunted for the cases that did not fit, and let the evidence overrule the fashionable belief. A single removed pump handle became a lasting lesson that careful observation can save lives.
